How I Built a Ride Dispatch Backend (In Simple Words)

System DesignMay 4, 2026· 8 min read

Most backend projects look great until they have to make a decision in real time.

A ride dispatch system is one of those real-time decision systems. It has to answer a simple question, very quickly:

"A rider needs a trip right now — which nearby driver should get it?"

I built this project to solve that exact problem in a practical way, using tools that are common in production systems.

What this project does

Think of this backend as a digital traffic controller for rides.

  • Riders send trip requests.
  • Drivers keep sharing live location.
  • The system finds the best nearby driver.
  • A trip is assigned and tracked.
  • Other systems are notified through events.

While the app looks simple from outside, inside it is balancing speed, correctness, and scalability all at the same time.

Why I chose this architecture

I did not use one database for everything. Instead, I split responsibilities based on what each data store is genuinely good at.

1) PostgreSQL — for reliable history

PostgreSQL stores long-term business records like ride requests, assignments, and driver availability. This is the source of truth. If anything else goes wrong, PostgreSQL has the ground reality.

2) Redis GEO — for speed

When a rider requests a trip, we cannot scan every driver row slowly. Redis GEO lets us find drivers near a pickup location in milliseconds. It is basically a spatial index that lives in memory.

3) Kafka — for communication between systems

After an assignment happens, other systems may need updates — analytics, notifications, billing. Kafka helps publish events so those systems can react independently without coupling them to the dispatch core.

4) Spring Boot — the orchestrator

Spring Boot is the layer that connects everything: API calls come in, business logic runs, PostgreSQL gets updated, Redis gets queried, Kafka gets published to. It is the glue.

Step-by-step: What happens when a rider books a trip

Here is the real flow in plain language:

  1. Rider sends a ride request to the API.
  2. System checks idempotency key (req:<requestId>) in Redis — this prevents duplicate trips when mobile apps retry.
  3. Ride request is saved in PostgreSQL.
  4. System asks Redis GEO: "Which drivers are near this pickup point?"
  5. Nearby drivers are filtered — available status only, matching tier if needed.
  6. Candidates are scored using distance + driver rating.
  7. Best driver is selected.
  8. Assignment is created in the database.
  9. Driver is marked unavailable.
  10. driver-assigned event is published to Kafka.

The result: one clear, fast assignment path that is easy to extend or debug.

What makes this project practical

Idempotency — retry safety

Mobile networks fail often. Without idempotency, one tap can create multiple trips. I added Redis-based request keys with TTL to prevent that. If the same request comes in twice, the second one gets the same result without re-running the logic.

Real-time geo matching

Redis GEO gives quick nearby-driver queries. This is critical — riders care about wait time, and slow matching means frustration before the trip even starts.

Separation of concerns

Transactional data stays in PostgreSQL. Hot geo lookups stay in Redis. Event fan-out is handled by Kafka. This keeps the system clean — changing one part does not break the others.

Extendable design

Because assignment emits Kafka events, new features can be added without rewriting dispatch core. Want to add a notification service? Subscribe to the Kafka topic. Want analytics? Same thing.

Challenges I noticed while building

No real system is perfect on the first version. These are the important tradeoffs I documented:

  • Concurrency risk: two requests might try to assign the same driver at the same time if locking is weak. This needs careful transaction handling.
  • Redis dependency: if location updates are stale or Redis goes down, matching quality drops. A fallback strategy matters.
  • Scale pressure: large candidate sets can increase database reads. Caching driver metadata in Redis helps reduce this.

Documenting these tradeoffs was important — production engineering is as much about knowing your limits as it is about shipping features.

What I would improve next

  1. Add stronger transaction locking for assignment safety.
  2. Add automatic re-dispatch when a driver declines or times out.
  3. Cache richer driver metadata in Redis to reduce DB lookups.
  4. Add metrics dashboards — match latency, success %, retry hit rate.
  5. Use the outbox pattern for stronger DB-to-Kafka delivery guarantees.

Final thoughts

This project is a good example of how I think as a backend engineer:

  • Start with a real user problem.
  • Choose tools based on workload, not hype.
  • Design for clarity first, then add reliability and scale patterns.
Built a real-time ride dispatch backend using Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, Redis GEO, and Kafka — with idempotent request handling, nearest-driver matching, and event-driven assignment workflows.

Scaling Spring Boot: Beyond the Defaults

JavaMar 2025· 6 min read

Spring Boot is incredibly easy to get started with. You add a few annotations, run the app, and it just works. But that ease comes with a hidden cost — the default settings are tuned for development, not production.

When real traffic hits, those defaults start to show their limits. Here's what I've learned about tuning Spring Boot for scale.

The problem with defaults

Spring Boot ships with sensible defaults that work fine on your laptop. But a laptop is not production. In production, you have hundreds or thousands of concurrent requests, database connection pools under pressure, and latency requirements that don't forgive.

Three areas matter most: thread pools, database connections, and Tomcat settings.

Thread pool tuning

Spring Boot's default executor uses a very small core thread pool. Under burst load, tasks start queuing up and response times climb.

The fix is to configure a custom ThreadPoolTaskExecutor based on your actual workload. CPU-bound tasks want fewer threads. IO-bound tasks — like most web services — can handle more.

A common starting point for IO-bound services: core pool size of 2x CPU cores, max pool size of 4x, with a bounded queue to apply backpressure instead of silently dropping work.

HikariCP — the connection pool you're already using

Spring Boot uses HikariCP by default, which is good — it is one of the fastest connection pools available. But the default maximumPoolSize is 10, which is often too low for services under real load.

The right pool size depends on your database server's capacity and your query latency. A rough formula: pool size = (core count × 2) + effective spindle count. For most cloud databases, this lands between 20 and 50 connections per service instance.

Also set connectionTimeout aggressively — failing fast is better than queuing requests that will time out anyway.

Tomcat connector settings

The embedded Tomcat server has a default max thread count of 200. For most services this is fine, but if you're seeing thread starvation under load, it's worth increasing — or better yet, switching to reactive/non-blocking with Spring WebFlux if your workload is heavily IO-bound.

The acceptCount setting controls how many connections queue when all threads are busy. Set it too high and you're just delaying failures. Set it too low and you reject valid requests. Finding the right value requires load testing your specific service.

What actually matters

All of this tuning is secondary to one thing: measuring first. Use Actuator metrics, Micrometer, and your APM of choice to understand where your service is actually spending time before you start changing numbers.

The engineers who get in trouble are the ones who tune blindly. The ones who scale well are the ones who measure, change one thing, measure again, and repeat.

Final thoughts

Spring Boot's defaults are a starting point, not a destination. Understanding what's under the hood — thread pools, connection management, server config — is the difference between a service that handles 100 rps and one that handles 10,000.

Start with measurement. Change one thing at a time. And always load test before you ship.

Database Tuning for the Impatient Engineer

DatabasesFeb 2025· 5 min read

Most database performance problems are not mysterious. They come down to the same handful of patterns: missing indexes, full table scans, N+1 queries, and bad query plans. Fix those and you're most of the way there.

This is a practical guide to the 20% of database work that gives you 80% of the gains.

Start with EXPLAIN ANALYZE

Before you do anything else, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on your slow queries. This tells you exactly what the database is doing — which indexes it's using (or not), how many rows it's scanning, and where the time is going.

The most important thing to look for: sequential scans on large tables. That's almost always a missing index. The second thing: high row estimates that don't match reality. That's stale statistics — fix it with ANALYZE.

Indexing — the high-leverage work

The right index on the right column is worth more than almost any other optimization. But indexes are not free — they slow down writes and take up space. So be deliberate.

Index columns that appear in WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, and ORDER BY. For compound indexes, the column order matters — put the most selective column first.

Partial indexes are underused. If you're always querying WHERE status = 'active' on a table where 95% of rows are inactive, a partial index on active rows only is dramatically smaller and faster.

The N+1 problem

This is the most common performance bug I see in application code. You load a list of 100 orders, then for each order you make a separate query to load the customer. That's 101 queries instead of one join.

ORMs make this easy to write and hard to notice until you're in production. The fix is eager loading or batch loading — in JPA, use JOIN FETCH or @BatchSize. And add query logging in development so you can see every SQL statement your application is generating.

Connection pool behavior under load

A slow query doesn't just affect one request — it holds a database connection for the duration. If your pool is small and your queries are slow, connections run out, requests queue, and latency spikes cascade across the service.

This is why query latency and connection pool health need to be monitored together. A sudden spike in p99 latency often means pool exhaustion, not just slow queries.

What to do this week

  1. Enable slow query logging — any query over 100ms should be reviewed.
  2. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on your top five slowest queries.
  3. Check for missing indexes on foreign keys — this is shockingly common.
  4. Add connection pool metrics to your dashboards.
  5. Review your ORM-generated queries in development — not just in production when it's too late.

Database performance is rarely glamorous, but it is one of the highest-leverage things you can work on as a backend engineer.

Distributed Tracing Without the Headache

ObservabilityJan 2025· 5 min read

Debugging a monolith is annoying. Debugging microservices without tracing is a nightmare.

When a request touches six services before returning an error, logs alone won't tell you which service caused the problem or how much time each hop took. Distributed tracing solves this — but getting it set up often feels harder than it should be.

Here's a practical approach that doesn't require turning your entire codebase into observability scaffolding.

What distributed tracing actually is

A trace is the story of one request as it travels through your system. Each step — a database call, an HTTP request to another service, a Kafka publish — becomes a span. Spans are nested and timed. Together they form a tree that shows you exactly where time was spent.

The key piece is a trace ID that propagates across service boundaries, so all the spans from one user request can be stitched together later.

OpenTelemetry is the right foundation

OpenTelemetry has become the standard. It's vendor-neutral, well-supported, and integrates with most backends — Jaeger, Zipkin, Grafana Tempo, Datadog, and others.

For Spring Boot services, the spring-boot-starter-actuator with Micrometer Tracing and the OpenTelemetry bridge gets you 80% of the way there with minimal code changes. Auto-instrumentation handles HTTP requests, JDBC calls, and Spring Kafka automatically.

The propagation problem

Tracing breaks if trace IDs don't cross service boundaries. For HTTP services, this is usually handled automatically via W3C TraceContext headers. For Kafka, you need to manually propagate headers in your producer and extract them in your consumer.

This is the step most teams miss. Without it, your traces end at the Kafka boundary and you lose visibility into the async processing side.

What to trace and what to skip

Not everything needs a span. Tracing has overhead — sampling helps manage this. A 10% sample rate in production is usually enough to surface patterns without crushing your tracing backend with volume.

Focus trace detail on: external service calls, database queries, cache lookups, and message queue operations. Skip: trivial utility functions, logging calls, config reads.

The practical starting point

  1. Add OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation to your services.
  2. Stand up a local Jaeger instance with Docker for development.
  3. Make sure trace IDs appear in your logs — structured logging with a trace ID field makes correlation trivial.
  4. Add manual spans for any business logic that doesn't get auto-instrumented.
  5. Set up sampling — 100% in development, 10% in production as a starting point.

Once you've traced one incident with this setup, you won't want to go back. The time saved on debugging pays for the setup effort within the first week.

Final thoughts

Distributed tracing is not a luxury for large teams. Even a two-service system benefits from traces. The question is not whether to add tracing — it's how to do it without it becoming a maintenance burden.

Start with auto-instrumentation, add sampling, and invest in trace ID propagation across async boundaries. That's the 80% that matters.
